Reverse osmosis is the only household filter that removes all four: PFAS, microplastics, lead and fluoride.

Everything else covers a subset, which is fine once you know which subset you need. Swipe for what each filter type actually does.

The certification numbers are where most people get lost. NSF 401 covers microplastics. 53 covers lead and PFAS on carbon. 58 covers reverse osmosis. P473 covers PFOA and PFOS. A filter certified only to 42 has been checked for chlorine and taste, and nothing else.

Polyester is plastic, and every wash sheds hundreds of thousands of microplastic fibres.

The part most people miss is where they go. Those fibres end up in indoor air and house dust as much as in waterways, which is how you end up breathing them rather than just flushing them away.

Washing cold, running fuller loads and washing less often all reduce shedding measurably. A filter bag catches a good share of the rest. None of it requires replacing your wardrobe.

The part of chewing gum that never gets smaller is a plastic polymer.

It comes from the same family used in glue and industrial coatings, and a 2025 UCLA study measured hundreds to thousands of microplastic fragments released into saliva per piece.

What makes it hard to avoid is the label. All of it hides behind one ingredient line reading gum base, and none of the polymers have to be named individually.

Chicle is the original gum base: tree sap, not polymer. A few brands still use it and say so plainly.

BPA free does not mean safe.

Manufacturers removed BPA and dropped in BPS and BPF, which are structurally similar and show comparable hormonal activity in lab studies. The label changed. The chemistry barely did.

It is a textbook regrettable substitution: swap a chemical people have heard of for one they have not, then keep the reassuring claim on the front of the pack.

Skip the claim and check the material instead. Glass and stainless steel do not need a chemical free badge, because there is no chemistry to disclose.
